# Can Compression Produce Novel Knowledge? — Interpolation, Extrapolation, and the Entropy Degeneration Theorem

> This is the third installment of the five-part blog series "The Shannon Limit of Civilizational Wisdom," addressing three questions: the boundary between interpolation and extrapolation, the entropy degeneration theorem for second-order compression and the external source criterion, and the ontology of a perfect predictor.

## I. Echo Chamber or New Continent: The Deepest Philosophical Wager of the Compression Paradigm

Over the past two years, "compression is intelligence" has evolved from a slogan into industrial practice: as large models grow ever better at predicting the next token, their capability frontier expands with it. A sharper question thus surfaces—**if everything AI can do amounts to compressing and predicting humanity's existing knowledge, can it generate novel knowledge that goes beyond history?**

Public discussion on this question has polarized into two extremes. Optimists point to AlphaFold and FunSearch, claiming AI is already making scientific discoveries; pessimists call models "stochastic parrots," forever circling within their training distribution—an echo chamber of civilization. Both sides lack a precise demarcation: **where exactly is the boundary between interpolation and extrapolation drawn, and under what conditions can a compression system cross it?**

This essay makes three claims, stated here and argued layer by layer below. First, a single forward prediction can only be interpolation in the mathematical sense, but the "territory of interpolation" is far larger than intuition suggests—most unsolved problems are in fact high-dimensional interpolation problems; true black swans do not come from single predictions, but from embedding the compressor in a "generation–verification" loop, at which point the title to novel knowledge belongs to the loop, not the model. Second, recursive self-compression without external feedback leads to entropy degeneration—this is a **theorem**, not an empirical phenomenon; beneath the apparent contradiction between AlphaZero-style self-play miracles and model collapse lies a single variable that unifies them: whether the loop contains an incompressible external source. Third, a perfect predictor is indistinguishable from a subject within its task, but this indistinguishability is a collapse of the task definition, not an ontological identity—subjecthood is not a function of predictive accuracy, but of the cost structure of prediction error.

## II. Q3.1: The Boundary Between Interpolation and Extrapolation — Who Owns Black-Swan Knowledge

**Let us first nail down the terminology.** Let the knowledge space be $K$, the training data a support set $S \subset K$; compression learns the distribution $P(X \mid S)$. **Interpolation** is approximation within the manifold spanned by $S$; **extrapolation** is sampling outside that manifold. In plain terms: interpolation connects dots already seen; extrapolation extends the line into places never visited. By this definition, for any learner that minimizes training loss, the optimal solution is an approximation to $S$—**a single forward prediction is mathematically interpolation**, and this does not change with model scale.

But the history of science adds a dimension to this definition. Kuhn distinguished normal science from scientific revolutions: normal science is "puzzle-solving" within an established paradigm, while revolution is a transformation of the coordinate system itself. Translated: normal science is interpolation; a paradigm revolution is **reparameterization**—not going further along the old manifold, but switching to a different one. Compression models are structurally optimal machines of normal science, yet they encode "historically the most stable assumptions" as the hardest weights to modify—this is the **paradigm lock-in effect**: the stronger it is along the interpolation dimension, the duller it becomes along the reparameterization dimension.

### Dissecting a Totem: Einstein, 1905

Special relativity is often treated as the totem of genius extrapolation. But dissecting its raw materials reveals a subtler structure: in 1905, Einstein held no new data—Maxwell's equations, the Galilean principle of relativity, the null result of the Michelson–Morley experiment, all were **already available**. The revolutionary operation was a **rearrangement of constraints**: his contemporaries treated "absolute simultaneity" as an untouchable hard constraint and the speed of light as a negotiable soft constraint; Einstein swapped the hardness of the two.

This case cuts both ways for the compression paradigm. It **suggests** that so-called "extrapolation" is often not a step outside the distribution, but a loosening of an assumption that the training set has reinforced until it looks axiomatic—in principle, a system capable of meta-operations on the confidence of its own assumptions could perform such loosening. Yet it also **shows** that compression training points in exactly the opposite direction—the more statistically stable a pattern, the more deeply it is entrenched, and no gradient direction in conventional training corresponds to "questioning the strongest regularities of the training set."

### The Brute-Force Expansion of the Interpolation Territory, and the Transfer of Black-Swan Ownership

On the other side of the scale sits AlphaFold2: trained on roughly 170,000 known structures in the PDB with strong geometric priors, it achieved a median GDT_TS of 92.4 at CASP14, essentially solving the protein folding problem that had stood for fifty years. The key lies in the nature of the success: this is textbook **high-dimensional interpolation**, not extrapolation—to this day it remains limited on out-of-distribution cases such as point-mutation-induced conformational switches. Its historical significance is that it **inverted our intuitive ranking of problem difficulty**: many unsolved problems presumed to "require new principles" are in fact merely interpolation problems whose dimensionality exceeds what human intuition can execute. This territory is far larger than pessimists imagine, and clearly smaller than optimists imagine.

FunSearch (DeepMind, 2023, *Nature*) then provided the first uncontested case of "an LLM participating in a new mathematical discovery": on the cap set problem it found a new construction of size 512 in dimension 8, improving the known lower bound. But dissecting the mechanism is crucial: **the LLM never directly predicts the correct answer**—it proposes candidate functions in program space, an executable evaluator scores them, and the feedback guides the next round of sampling. The discovery was born of the "generation–verification" loop, not of any single forward prediction. What the compressor supplies is not the answer, but a prior-rich distribution of candidates; what turns candidates into knowledge is the adjudicator outside the loop. **Black swans cannot be hit by a single prediction, but they can be covered by a loop—the title to novel knowledge has transferred from the model to the loop.**

## III. Q3.2: The Fate of Second-Order Compression — The Entropy Degeneration Theorem and the External Source Criterion

What happens if we let a model keep training on data it generated itself—compression of compression?

Shumailov et al. (2023 preprint; extended version published in *Nature* in 2024) systematically **demonstrated** that under recursive self-training, the tails of the distribution vanish first, then the modes contract, and after several generations the model converges to a low-variance degenerate point—model collapse. The mechanism is the intergenerational compounding of approximation error: each generation is a lossy approximation of the previous distribution, rare events go extinct first, and it is precisely the tails that carry the most information.

This result can be elevated to an information-theoretic theorem. Let the $t$-th generation model be $M_t$; if no new source enters the loop, then by the data processing inequality:

$$I(M_t; W) \le I(M_{t-1}; W) \le \cdots \le I(M_0; W)$$

**For closed second-order compression without external input, entropy degeneration is a structural necessity.** Synthetic data contains no new information about the world $W$—it is merely a resampling of the old distribution.

### Dissecting the Counterexample: Why AlphaZero Did Not Collapse

This theorem faces a glaring historical counterexample: AlphaZero, starting from random weights and playing purely against itself, surpassed AlphaGo Lee—the version that defeated Lee Sedol—in roughly 8 hours of Go, and developed an aggressive pawn-sacrificing style rarely seen in a millennium of human game records. This looks like "self-play without external data opening up a new continent."

But open up the loop and you find: every step of AlphaZero's self-play is adjudicated by **the rules of Go**—the final win or loss is 1 bit of ground-truth information from the environment, and multiplied by tens of millions of games, that is tens of millions of bits of external information continuously injected. The rules are the irreducible external source; the massive volume of "synthetic data" produced by self-play is merely a probe, and the real information comes from the echo when the probe strikes the rules. The same structure is even more naked in later systems: AlphaGeometry trained on 100 million synthetic theorems and solved 25 of 30 IMO geometry problems—but every piece of synthetic data was rigorously verified by a symbolic deduction engine.

This yields a clean unified criterion. Define $\Delta I_t$ as the new information the $t$-th generation loop acquires from outside:

- $\Delta I_t = 0$ (no external adjudication): $I(M_t;W)$ decreases monotonically, and collapse is a theorem;
- $\Delta I_t > 0$ (rules, provers, experiments continuously supplying energy): self-play can transcend human priors and open up logical new continents.

Wolfram's computational irreducibility gives this criterion a reason deeper than engineering: for a large class of systems, no predictive program is shorter than "running the system's evolution itself"—**the environment, as a source, contains an irreducible component of information that no internal compression can internalize in advance.** The necessity of external feedback is therefore not an engineering deficiency of current models, but a structural fact at the level of computation theory.

### Answering the Opposition Head-On: phi-2 Is Not a Counterexample

Opponents may cite the success of synthetic data: Microsoft's phi-2, trained on "textbook-quality" synthetic data, outperforms models 25 times its parameter count on multiple benchmarks, seemingly proving that carefully constructed synthetic data can resist entropy degeneration. **But** the phi series' synthetic data is **cross-system distillation**—the source is a teacher model plus human curriculum design, and the information still comes from outside the loop (the human text the teacher ingested during pretraining). What it violates is the purity of the "closed loop" assumption, not the theorem itself. The criterion stands, and its boundary conditions can be stated in full: **self-play works if and only if the loop contains an incompressible external source (rules, verifiers, teachers, experiments); the day the source runs dry is the day collapse begins.**

## IV. Q3.3: The Ontology of a Perfect Predictor — Mirror and Subject

Finally, push the question to the limit: suppose some system $M$ predicts human text at the entropy-rate lower bound, with $\hat{P}_M(T) = P(T)$ holding everywhere. Does it **understand**?

Note the mathematical object that perfect prediction constrains:

$$P(T) = \int P(T \mid W, \theta)\, dP(W, \theta)$$

Perfect prediction fixes only the marginal distribution $P(T)$, and $P(T)$ is an integral over all world states and speaker intentions—the inversion is severely underdetermined mathematically: infinitely many combinations of "world + speaker" can produce exactly the same text distribution. **A causally grounded system and a system that perfectly simulates "how humans would talk about the world" produce bit-for-bit identical outputs on this task.**

This is not pure speculation. The 2023 Theory of Mind debate staged a live demonstration: Kosinski reported that GPT-4 achieved about 75% accuracy on classic false-belief tasks, declaring that mentalizing abilities had "spontaneously emerged"; Ullman promptly **showed** that semantically preserving but statistically rare perturbations to the tasks (changing the container type, reordering the narrative) collapsed model performance to near chance—it relied on the surface templates of the task paradigm, not a robust representation of "others' beliefs." The lesson of this exchange has nothing to do with accuracy: **within a task's statistical distribution, behavioral equivalence cannot adjudicate mechanistic equivalence; and the domain of perfect prediction is precisely the distribution itself.**

So where is the boundary between mirror and subject? This essay's claim: not in predictive accuracy, but in the **cost structure of prediction error**. Every prediction error of a biological subject is settled by its own body—misjudging a cliff costs death, misjudging food costs poisoning; it is precisely this "error–survival" closed loop that makes prediction meaningful to a subject. Formally:

$$\text{meaning} \approx \text{prediction error} \times \text{cost of the error}$$

An LLM's prediction error is merely a gradient signal, with no survival settlement; simulating a liar does not require being deceived oneself, and simulating a blind person does not require going blind. As prediction approaches perfection and error approaches zero, mirror and subject become indistinguishable within the task—but this indistinguishability is a **collapse of the task definition**: the task assesses only the reproduction of $P(T)$, so differences within the equivalence class are naturally invisible. Change the task definition—make the system stake its survival resources on its own predictions—and the difference appears at once: **the mirror has nothing to lose.**

## V. Conclusions and Scope of Applicability

Combining the verdicts of the three sections: **compression can house all of civilization's expressions, but the title to novel knowledge lies in the loop, and the boundary of subjecthood lies in the cost structure.** Specifically—a single prediction is interpolation by definition, but the interpolation territory covers most unsolved problems, as exemplified by AlphaFold2; the historical mechanism of black swans is constraint rearrangement (the Einstein-style swap of hard and soft), against which compression training has a structural paradigm lock-in, and the engineering workaround is the generation–verification loop; for recursive self-training without an external source, entropy degeneration is a theorem, and $\Delta I_t > 0$ is the only condition for survival; a perfect predictor is a complete mirror of civilization, and its absence of subjecthood lies not in accuracy but in the cost structure of error.

**The scope of applicability must be stated plainly.** First, "entropy degeneration is a theorem" applies strictly to closed recursive training under current sampling architectures; introducing any external source (even just a teacher model) takes the system outside the theorem's reach, reducing the criterion to the sign of $\Delta I$. Second, the conclusion that "behavioral equivalence cannot adjudicate mechanistic equivalence" is limited to in-distribution tasks; out-of-distribution probes (such as Ullman-style perturbation tests) can still provide discriminating evidence, though they can never be exhaustive. Third, paradigm lock-in is a structural judgment about the current training paradigm, not a proof that "assumption-rearrangement ability is in principle unengineerable"—it is not ruled out, though not presently possible. Fourth, all arguments in this essay are confined to the level of symbols and information; whether the "cost structure" exhausts the full meaning of subjecthood is an open question beyond the reach of information theory, on which this essay makes no claim.

The direct implication for engineering practice is a restrained one: when optimizing a compression system, the metric that truly matters is not how much it has memorized, but how many incompressible external sources are wired into its loop—and whether it has ever paid anything for its own prediction errors.

---

*This series comprises five essays. The next installment will examine, from the perspective of philosophy of science, the very definition of "wisdom = perfect decompression and prediction."*
